To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
SES is positively related to sensitivity, with this relation being stronger among Chinese mothers than Malay mothers.
SES was a significant positive predictor of sensitivity, and this relation was moderated by ethnicity.
SES was positively associated with sensitivity in Chinese mothers, but not Malay and Indian mothers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how ethnicity and socioeconomic status influence parenting behavior in a Southeast Asian context.
how culture and ethnicity moderate the SES-sensitivity link in a non-Western sample.
how culture influences the relation between SES, perceived stress, and parenting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SES is associated with maternal sensitivity, but the nature of this relation may vary by ethnicity.
ethnicity does not moderate the relation between SES, but SES positively predicts sensitivity in Chinese dyads and may marginally predict sensitivity in Indian dyads, but not Malay.
SES positively predicts parenting sensitivity in Chinese, and possibly Indian dyads, but not Malay ones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ethnicity and SES interact to influence maternal sensitivity, but that this relation may be more complex than previously thought.

SES and ethnicity are not mutually exclusive predictors of parenting behavior in Singapore, and that the relation between SES, ethnicity, and parenting is likely to be complex and contextually dependent.
SES and education may be more salient predictors of parenting sensitivity for Chinese than Malay dyads.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethnicity and socioeconomic status interact to influence parenting sensitivity in a Southeast Asian context.
ethnicity may moderate the association between SES and maternal sensitivity.
ethnicity and SES should be assessed simultaneously in Asian contexts.
